The 10-year is -3bp since the hike vs a +18bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 804bp against a five-year average of 415bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +33bp and BB +24bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.33 → 0.62 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Pre-market tone is constructive. S&P futures (ES) are at 7744.75, +0.39%, and Nasdaq futures are +0.59%, following Monday's cash session: S&P 500 +0.70% to 7676.77, Nasdaq Comp +0.82%, Dow +0.28%, Russell +0.38%. VIX eased to 17.78 from 18.39. Overseas, the Nikkei rallied +1.73% to 63268.37 and the Euro Stoxx 50 is +0.33%. The FTSE 100 lags at -0.89%. The day's macro event is the Fed: the FOMC meets Oct 27-28 after September's 25bp hike to 3.75%-4%, and reports put the odds of another hike this month at only about 15% (itiger, tradingeconomics). Bonds are steady: the 10Y is at 4.9864%, the 2Y at 4.7245% and the 30Y at 5.2953%. The biggest story underneath the calm equity tape is credit. The Caa-minus-B gap (how much more the weakest junk issuers pay than single-B issuers) is 804bp. That is 100th percentile vs the last five years, nearly double its 5y average of ~415bp, and the widest since 2020-04-15. It is up 117bp in a month and 255bp in three months, and the FRED CCC-B cross-check (1013bp) agrees. Is it spreading? Partly. Single-B OAS rose 33bp over 1m and Ba OAS 24bp, so the whole ladder drifted wider. But the B-Ba gap of 117bp sits below its 5y average (46th pct), and IG is still tight at 88bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.62 from 0.33 three months ago, which means the two are starting to move together more. It is still below its 5y median of 0.70. This is descriptive, not a validated signal: CCC rot is real but has not yet clearly jumped into BB or IG. Sentiment is complacent at the index level, with the S&P at a 99th-percentile stretch vs its own history (computed z 2.78), and Brent at 115.02 is a standing inflation tax. Megacap earnings this week (MSFT/GOOGL Oct 28, AMZN Oct 29, AAPL Nov 2 per Bloomberg dates) will decide whether the equity rally can keep ignoring credit.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 485.61 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is trading at 485.61 cents/gal, at the 99.8th percentile with a z-score of 3.29, so the front of the market is at a historic extreme. Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.76 vol points (45th percentile of the 53 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 102.2 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 86bp (steeper by 11bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (117bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 26 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Today's market resembles 2000 in what it costs and how few names carry it, not in how it trades. Shiller CAPE near 41 is close to the late-1999 peak of 44.2 (sources below). The market-cap/GDP ratio is reported above 236%, and the top ten names are reported above 35% of the S&P. On the computed side, the Nasdaq is only 4.7% above its 200DMA vs 50% at the 2000 peak, and retail sentiment is net-bearish (AAII -8.9pp), so the speculative blow-off phase is absent. The current cycle path (anchored Oct-2022, at 238.2 after 48 months) tracks the 1990-anchored dot-com run roughly two-thirds of the way to its peak month. The more relevant catalyst risk is not equity froth but credit: IG and Baa spreads are tighter than in 2000 even as the CCC tier blows out. That is the kind of divergence that tends to precede rather than follow a top. IPO froth (analyst estimate 55) reflects a large pipeline, including reports of a possible Anthropic listing, but not 2000-style day-one mania in the data I could verify.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the Oct 27-28 FOMC is the base case (inference). Mid-October CME pricing reportedly showed only ~15% odds of a hike, and Warsh's Bangkok remarks pushed traders to scale back hike bets further. A hike cannot be ruled out: he has said he does not prejudge meetings and named October and December as decision points.

~1 YEAR

Inference: a hawkish-leaning hold with optionality for one more hike. The September decision raised rates 25bp to 3.75%-4% unanimously, and a majority projected a further hike before year-end. Warsh has repeatedly stressed persistent inflation and the priority of reaching 2%. Cuts within ~12 months look unlikely unless the CCC credit stress or growth breaks. That is my analyst inference, not his stated guidance.

Warsh's on-record posture: inflation is not slowing enough, 2% remains the priority, and the world has 'broadly conformed' with Fed expectations. He refuses to pre-commit. With Core PCE at 3.00759, Flexible CPI rising, and the 2s10s at a computed 25.98bp, the data give him room to sit tight today. The 2Y at 4.7245% vs a 3.75%-4% funds range shows the market still embeds tightening risk. Flag: reports differ on the September dot count (majority vs 16 of 18), and one older source still lists the pre-hike range, which I disregard.
